product_description: Headless hollow thin-skin electric guitar with an embedded Linux host, intended as a practice and travel instrument rather than a stage instrument. The modern electric campfire guitar: played with headphones or wirelessly, with onboard effects and a coaching engine.

construction.body_architecture_note: Two composite skins over a hollow wooden core with a structural frame and centre block, in the manner of the Masonite-era Danelectro. The hollow interior is what makes the full electronics package fit; the same stack has no valid placement in a solid body of these dimensions.

series.note: The only series for this product line. Headless suits a practice and travel instrument: shorter overall length, no headstock to knock, tuning at the bridge.

components: Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB) — JACK + Guitarix/MODEP host and coaching engine
HiFiBerry DAC+ADC — I2S audio out and headphone jack
Teensy 4.1 — I/O coprocessor, control only, no audio path
Battery pack + BMS (4x 18650), USB-C PD 20 W charging
40 mm cooling fan, lid-mounted, venting outward
GPIO ribbon between the Pi and the HAT
electronics_package.rationale: The full stack including the HiFiBerry HAT, because the headphone jack is the point of a practice instrument. The hollow box provides the volume: the same package is 96 cm2 short of fitting a solid body of these dimensions.
electronics_package.open_question: AUDIO FRONT END UNRESOLVED. The canonical signal chain routes input through an external Hi-Z USB interface, so this instrument has never actually been self-contained — the HiFiBerry HAT provides output only. Replacing the HAT with a converter board plus a discrete front end is NOT a cheap substitution: it would require designing a Hi-Z input stage, instrument preamp, gain control, headphone amplifier, protection circuitry and analog filtering, all of which a USB interface already solves. The question for a practice and campfire instrument is therefore not whether to use an interface but whether one small enough to mount INSIDE the body exists. Derived envelope: about 150 x 70 x 36 mm and under roughly 120 cm2 of pocket footprint. Height is the hard limit at 36 mm — 47 mm blank less 8 mm floor and 3 mm lid clearance. The MOTU M2 at 45 mm and the Scarlett Solo at 47 mm both exceed it; a compact two-input class device at around 105 x 45 x 25 mm would fit comfortably in either product line.

materials.body: hollow wooden core, species not yet selected
materials.skins: composite / hardboard, thickness not yet selected

provenance.note: Split from a single conflated product record on 2026-07-27, when the practice and performance lines were separated.

notes: STATUS IS 'concept', NOT 'draft'. The Smart Guitar is still an AI-generated photograph. Every dimension derived so far is real arithmetic performed on an imagined object: the outline is corroborated for proportion across three artifacts but has never been measured against a physical blank, and the cavity datum is an engineering fit rather than a measurement.
This is explicitly NOT a performance instrument. It is a practice and travel instrument, so headphone output matters and stage ergonomics do not.
Body construction changes the economics as well as the packing. Thin-skin over a hollow core weighs about 48% of solid Khaya at the same dimensions, so body size is not constrained by weight here.

The through-body ergonomic voids are the visual identity of this instrument and are deliberately NOT reduced. They double the finished edge length, from 1.51 m of outer perimeter to 3.01 m including void edges on both faces, which lands directly on the edge-cleanup and edge-sealing operations already identified as the cost risk in the thin-skin estimate. Roughly 48 minutes and $23 per unit, and worth paying.
Core species, skin material and thickness, and the finish system are all unselected. They are the remaining inputs to the budget model, not settled facts.
Contains no cost, price, or margin fields by design.

The 'campfire guitar' premise depends on an onboard audio interface. With an external box this instrument is a desk practice tool, not a travel one. That is a product decision, not an engineering one, and it is unresolved.
